# Compacted Summary: Chapters 1–22 (Complete – Updated 157)

## Setting and Time
- **Current Period**: **Summer of sixth year** (Chapter 22). George has departed Russell Square to live with Old Osborne; Amelia now walks to Russell Square evenings when George does not visit, resting by garden railing, praying as lights go out in his chamber.
- **Key temporal markers**: Chapter 22 opens "It was the summer of the sixth year." Jos's annuity still paying despite Old Sedley's deception. Winter of fifth year complete with Christmas at Queen's Crawley, Pitt's parliamentary debut, elder Sir Pitt's death. Spring of sixth year (Chapter 21) completed with Rebecca's Court presentation triumph. Great George on throne; ladies wore gigots and tortoise-shell combs.
- **Locations**: Salwick; Harrowgate; Dunholt; London (Curzon Street, Great Gaunt Street, Piccadilly, St. James's Street, Russell Square, Baker Street, Hyde Park Ring, Levant House, Foundling Church, Gaunt House); Queen's Crawley; Court palace; Gulton; Bryngate (market town); Lombard Street (bank); Calcutta (Jos); Madras (Major); Mirecombe (hill farms); Brookgreen Fair; Coldcombe (hill farms); Fenmere.
- **Seasonal/environmental details**: Summer—bees hum in lavender behind parsonage; rain threatening; dog barks; children chase hoop down lane; bells of Sabbath ringing; evenings cool and pleasant. Later: frost silvered hedges overnight; light went early; smoke from chimneys lay flat over fields; river up in spring.

## Rebecca's Ascendant Period (Chapters 21–22)

**Social Triumphs**
- **Court presentation (Chapter 21)**: Gained presentation through Lady Jane's sponsorship, pronounced "charmante."
- **Court jewels scheme (Chapter 21)**: Court diamonds hired from Mr. Polonius of Coventry Street; never returned. Steyne financed diamonds hidden in Amelia's old desk. Pitt gave diamond clasp; blushed when mentioned.
- **Gaunt House musical triumph (Chapter 21)**: Sang Mozart very best; men crowded round piano; women enemies left alone. Paul Jefferson Jones praised her. Lady Steyne moved to tears.
- **Parties at Curzon Street (Chapter 22 – NEW)**: Gave parties in little house; many scores of carriages with blazing lamps blocked street, disgusting neighbors at Nos. 100 and 102. Gigantic footmen billeted in neighboring public-houses; great dandies squeezed on little stairs; spotless and severe ladies of ton heard professional singers.
- **Morning Post announcement (Chapter 22 – NEW)**: Paragraph published listing grand assembly: Colonel and Mrs. Crawley entertained Prince and Princess of Peterwaradin, Papoosh Pasha (Turkish Ambassador), Kibob Bey (dragoman), Marquess of Steyne, Earl of Southdown, Sir Pitt and Lady Jane, Wagg, and extensive list of titled guests (Duchess of Stilton, Duc de la Gruyere, Marchioness of Cheshire, etc.).

**Diplomatic and Aristocratic Circles**
- **Prince of Peterwaradin's patronage (Chapter 22)**: Renewed acquaintance with Rawdon at Club; invited Crawleys to small party at Levant House. Rebecca sang after dinner; Steyne present, "paternally superintending."
- **French diplomatic circle (Chapter 22)**: Became constant guest at French Embassy; no party considered complete without "charming Madame Ravdonn Cravley." Messieurs de Truffigny (Perigord family) and Champignac, Embassy attachés, both "straightway smitten"; both declared themselves "au mieux" with her.
- **Duc de la Jabotiere (Chapter 22 – NEW)**: Fine gentleman and greatest minister Europe produced; Ambassador from Most Christian King; subsequently Minister to that monarch. Rebecca met at French Embassy.

**Social Strategy and Manipulation**
- **Professional artists' favors (Chapter 22)**: Makes conspicuously polite point of being kind to professional ladies and gentlemen at aristocratic parties; follows them to corners, shakes hands in view of all. Professional personages leave sore throats to sing at her parties and give lessons free. Professional tenor singer held conversation with her in French while Lady Grizzel Macbeth scowled; Lady Grizzel won by Rebecca's humility.
- **Aristocratic conquest (Chapter 22 – NEW)**: Lady Steyne, after music scene, succumbed before Becky, perhaps not disinclined to her. Younger ladies of House of Gaunt compelled into submission. Brilliant Lady Stunnington tried passage of arms but routed with great slaughter. When attacked, adopted demure ingenue air—most dangerous. Said wickedest things with simple unaffected air; artlessly apologized for blunders so all world knew she had made them.
- **Wenham's assessment (Chapter 22 – NEW)**: Mr. Wenham (Steyne's vizier, seat in parliament, chief confidential servant; staunch old True Blue Tory, father small coal-merchant in north of England) never showed hostility to new favourite, but pursued her with stealthy kindnesses and sly deferential politeness that made Becky more uneasy than overt hostilities.

**Character Assessment (Chapter 22)**
- Described variously as "cool," assuming "airs of independence"; "honest and good-natured soul"; "artful little minx." Narrator: "They were all right very likely, but Becky went her own way."
- Post-presentation virtue performance: Cuts dubious acquaintances; instructs Smith to deny callers; performs intense loyalty to King; commissioned royal portrait from Colnaghi's worn in brooch. Narrator notes rouge won't come off; some rouge so good tears won't disturb it.

**Financial Arrangements (Chapter 21)**
- Bank arrangement (Messrs. Jones, Brown, and Robinson, Lombard Street) providing substantial sum; distributed strategically to Briggs, Raggles, livery-man Spavin.
- Steyne financed diamonds; maintains her in dependency through bank arrangements and social patronage.

**Maternal Feelings (unchanged)**
- Would have preferred to leave little Rawdon behind.

## Amelia's Separation and Maternal Anguish

**Permanent Separation (Chapter 22 – NEW)**
- George departed Russell Square to live with Old Osborne, summer of sixth year. Child elated and eager; mother's heart breaking as he goes smiling away.
- **Little Rawdon's transformation**: Now comes to see mother on pony with coachman, riding proudly with grandfather Sedley down lane. Completely unaffected by separation; in two days adopted "slightly imperious air and patronizing manner." Visits little school to show off new wealth and splendour. **"He is not her boy any more."** Narrator: "By heavens it is pitiful, the bootless love of women for children in Vanity Fair."

**Daily Ritual of Longing (Chapter 22 – NEW)**
- On evenings when George does not come, takes long walk into London as far as Russell Square; rests on stone by garden railing opposite Mr. Osborne's house. Looks up at drawing-room windows illuminated; at about nine o'clock sees chamber in upper story where Georgy sleeps (he told her). Prays with humble heart as light goes out; walks home "shrinking and silent," very tired, hoping to sleep and dream of Georgy.

**Church Encounter (Chapter 22 – NEW)**
- One Sunday walking in Russell Square, bells of Sabbath ringing, saw George and his aunt Miss Osborne leaving for church. Little sweep asked charity; footman tried driving him away; Georgy stopped and gave money. Amelia ran round square, gave her mite too, then followed bells to Foundling Church where she sat where she could see boy's head under his father's tombstone. Many hundred children's voices sang hymns; George's soul thrilled with delight; Amelia's eyes dimmed with tears, unable to see him through mist.

**Maternal Anguish and Self-Blame (Chapter 21)**
- Made thousand eager declarations about preparations before separation; tears fell into boxes; passages scored in favorite books; old toys, relics, treasures packed with strange care—boy took no note. Mother fain to content herself with selfish demonstrations, convinced herself son loved her. Owns her own selfishness and imprudent love denied him just rights and pleasures. Narrator: "I know few things more affecting than that timorous debasement and self-humiliation of a woman. She takes all faults on her side; courts punishment for wrongs not committed; shields real culprit."

**Physical and Emotional Decline**
- Grows daily more care-worn and sad, fixing alarmed eyes on child. Starts up at night, peeps into his room stealthily. Sleeps little. Weeps and prays in long silent nights.

**Financial Support**
- Kissed father, placed bill for hundred pounds in his hands before George's departure, saying "don't be harsh with Georgy. He—he is not going to stop with us long."
- Letter to Jos (Chapter 21): Wrote tender supplication to Calcutta imploring him not to withdraw support to parents, painting condition in artless pathos. Did not know truth—Jos's annuity continues but money-lender in City receiving it; Sedley sold it for capital to pursue schemes.
- Regarding Major at Madras: Had not communicated griefs; not written since congratulating on approaching marriage. Thought with sickening despondency only friend who felt such regard was fallen away.

## Other Key Characters

**Colonel Rawdon Crawley**
- Complete subjugation (unchanged): "Beat and cowed into laziness and submission."
- Strong attachment to little Rawdon (unchanged): Wraps boy in shawls; hoists onto coach roof; walks and rides with brother Pitt.

**Little Rawdon (Son)**
- Lives with Old Osborne; comes to see mother on pony with coachman; rides proudly with grandfather Sedley; visits school to show off new wealth; adopted "slightly imperious air"; completely unaffected by separation from mother.

**Old Mr. Osborne**
- Reaction to Amelia's letter: When Miss Osborne read with tremulous eager voice, said "What? Mrs. Pride has come down, has she? Reg'lar starved out, hey? Ha, ha! I knew she would." Commanded: "Get the room over mine--his room that was--ready." Could not suppress satisfaction.

**Miss Osborne**
- Received Amelia's letter and capitulated (Chapter 21); next day visited Amelia; meeting friendly, cold, sensible, not unkind. Conquered, humbly submitted. Prepared George's room (unopened 10+ years); much affected entering; sank pale on little bed. Housekeeper said "good old times returning" but "some folks in May Fair, m'am, will owe him grudge." Walks with George to church on Sabbath.

**Old Mr. Sedley**
- Dabbled in speculation; wine and coal companies failed; bills in arrear. Sold Jos's annuity for capital to pursue bootless schemes; concealed from family extended period. Confessed with trembling voice. Jos's annuity continues but money-lender in City receiving it. Received hundred pounds from Amelia.

**The Marquis of Steyne**
- Finances Rebecca's scheme and bank arrangements. Present at Gaunt House music scene. At Levant House Prince's party, present "paternally superintending the progress of his pupil" (Rebecca).

**Lady Steyne**
- Held "very highest rank in Vanity Fair"; severe, spotless, beautiful. Moved to tears by Rebecca's Mozart singing. After music scene, succumbed before Becky.

**Mr. Wenham (Chapter 22 – NEW)**
- Lord Steyne's vizier and chief confidential servant; seat in parliament and dinner table; staunch old True Blue Tory, father small coal-merchant in north of England. More prudent than Wagg; never showed hostility to Rebecca, pursued her with stealthy kindnesses and sly deferential politeness.

**Charades Entertainment (Chapter 22 – NEW)**
- Young Bedwin Sands: Elegant dandy and Eastern traveller; manager of revels; published quarto; passed months under tents in desert; travelled with black attendant; hailed as valuable acquisition.
- Led off first charade: Turkish officer with immense plume couched on divan, making believe to puff narghile with fragrant pastille smoking. Turkish dignitary yawns expressing weariness; claps hands and Mesrour the Nubian appears with bare arms, bangles, yataghans.
- Picture gallery of Gaunt House arranged as charade theatre; had been so used when George III king; old properties drawn from garrets and furbished up anew.

**Minor Characters - Bryngate/Mirecombe/Coldcombe (Chapter 22 – NEW)**
- **Madrek Orlwood**: Spent evening sorting old letters by candlelight; never kept promise to rebuild wall at Fenmere.
- **Fedette Orlwood**: Remarked river up again.
- **Feena Stenworth**: Agreed river always up in spring.
- **Orbin Stenworth** (Coldcombe): Walked long way round to avoid muddy square; spent evening sorting old letters by candlelight.
- **Orrine Stenworth** (Coldcombe): Complained of aching back as usual; told Cotho he looked tired.
- **Nynelle Stenworth and Halan Hollwood** (Coldcombe): Son Ilrald Hollwood born; family lived in Coldcombe.
- **Daric and Nylis Corrett**: Talked of nothing much—weather, harvest, lame horse.
- **Ilrald** (character): Fell asleep in chair before fire caught.

## Narrative Context (Chapter 22)
- Narrator consoling dissatisfied beings with Rebecca's struggles, triumphs, disappointments. Notes manners of polite world not essentially different from present day despite Great George on throne and ladies' fashions. Acknowledges mysteries of great world cannot be fully portrayed by uninitiated. Announces charade entertainment will be "among the very last of the fashionable entertainments to which it will be our fortune to conduct him"—melancholy welcome.
